body:

resolved_issues.title: Cosim mismatch when reading DCSR.cause
resolved_issues.body:
## Observed Behavior
Test failures with the following error : 
```
UVM_FATAL ibex_cosim_scoreboard.sv(138) @ 4049807: Cosim mismatch Register write data mismatch to x22 DUT: 40000100 expected: 400000c0
```

This fails upon reading from `DCSR.cause`
In this case : 

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/102029880/184605611-4f106a6b-a987-4952-b636-760647e12afe.png)
(IBEX)

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/102029880/184605563-b1bd1eb8-b8c3-47c2-b263-3c84427153f3.png)
(SPIKE)

Observing the waveform below, we can see that `debug_req_i` is de-asserted shortly after `debug_mode_i` goes low due to leaving debug mode from a dret. We do re-enter debug mode, but the cause can be seen to be recorded as `DBG_CAUSE_STEP`. In spike, we read back `DBG_CAUSE_HALTREQ` at the same instruction, hence the mismatch.

## Expected Behavior

Ibex should record `DCSR.cause` as DBG_CAUSE_HALTREQ.

I think this might be due to the [ibex_controller.sv ](https://github.com/lowRISC/ibex/blob/2f8dfa9dfe2d938228118ed8ab6a543804d0c9ae/rtl/ibex_controller.sv#L662)state machine sampling the `debug_req_i` signal to determine the correct `cause` one cycle later than the decision to enter debug_mode.

## Steps to reproduce the issue
```
cd dv/uvm/core_ibex/
make TEST=riscv_debug_basic_test ITERATIONS=1 WAVES=1 SEED=9892 -j12 -ik
```
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/102029880/184603232-ef1a9397-1cd2-4a0b-828b-1b2eb4e1745a.png)

> estimate 8
> remaining 2022-09-27 4

. /etc/profile.d/ibex-verilator.sh
git rev-parse HEAD > /tmp/ibex_baseline_commit
problem_statement: Reading the `cause` field of the RISC-V Debug Control and Status Register (`DCSR.cause`) can report the wrong reason for entering debug mode. In the failing behavior, Ibex records a single-step cause (`DBG_CAUSE_STEP`) even though debug mode was entered because of an external debug request (`debug_req_i`), which should be reported as `DBG_CAUSE_HALTREQ`. This affects the debug-entry cause recording logic in `ibex_controller`. The bug is triggered when the core decides to enter debug mode because `debug_req_i` is asserted, but `debug_req_i` is de-asserted before the later cycle that saves the cause into `DCSR.cause`; the issue was observed after a debug return instruction (`dret`) followed by immediate re-entry into debug mode. In that situation, `DCSR.cause` must still read back as `DBG_CAUSE_HALTREQ`, because the debug entry was caused by the halt request rather than by single-step execution.

title: [rtl] Do not register instruction fetch errors
body:
Registering instruction fetch errors causes problem in the case of seeing
a PMP execution access block. ID/EX stage learns about
the instruction that it executed should be blocked a
cycle late. This commit fixes that.

Found this one while working on fixing https://github.com/lowRISC/ibex/issues/1720. However it does not fully solves the issue because we are still seeing some mismatches because of some self modifying code problems.

Signed-off-by: Canberk Topal <ctopal@lowrisc.org>

repo.name: ibex
repo.description: Ibex is a small 32 bit RISC-V CPU core, previously known as zero-riscy.

commits.message:
[rtl] Flush controller in PMP CSR write ops

As Greg pointed out:

When we have an instruction in ID/EX that writes a PMP register that
update gets written to the CSR the same cycle the next instruction
moves from IF to ID/EX with it's PMP check done with the old value.

The solution is to flush the pipeline when we get a PMP CSR write.

Signed-off-by: Canberk Topal <ctopal@lowrisc.org>

problem_statement: Ibex can apply a Physical Memory Protection (PMP) update one instruction late. When software writes a PMP address or configuration CSR so that the next instruction address becomes non-executable, the core may still fetch that next instruction and let it execute instead of faulting immediately. The expected behavior is that the updated PMP permissions take effect for the very next instruction fetch: if the next program counter is now blocked for execution, that instruction must not execute and the core must raise an instruction access fault at that program counter. This bug affects PMP-based instruction-fetch permission checking, and it is triggered by a PMP CSR write immediately followed by a fetch from the newly blocked address.

title: Move not-taken, predicted taken branch address calculation to ID stage
body:
Currently, the not-taken address of a branch is registered in flops in the prefetch buffer or instruction cache when ever a branch prediction is lodged with these modules. However, as discussed in https://github.com/lowRISC/ibex/issues/1462, there is an issue with this address being overridden by a second predicted branch when the an instruction moves from the prefetch to the IF stage skid buffer. If the instruction in the skid buffer was mispredicted taken, the prefetch will replay from the stored address of the second predicted branch, not the first one.

To solve this without adding extra flops in the IF stage to store the not-taken address of the instruction in the skid buffer, we can get rid of these flops entirely and calculate the not-taken address in the ID stage. This would be fed back along with the existing not-taken mispredict signal `nt_branch_mispredict_i` used to clear the prefetch and allows it to resume fetching on the correct path.

As a code refactoring bonus, we do not need to consider the existence of the branch predictor in the prefetch buffer, instruction cache and fetch FIFO modules any more. Previously, the next address of the fetch FIFO would be registered in flops as the not-taken address using an `if generate` block based on the `BranchPredictor` parameter, but these flops do not exist anymore as of this PR.

Though not specifically relevant to this change, we now also suppress the validity of the skid buffer content by `nt_branch_mispredict_i` which prevents mispredicted instructions in the skid buffer from entering the ID stage. This is required as part of fixing the aforementioned bug.

problem_statement: When `BranchPredictor=1`, Ibex can mis-handle recovery from a branch that was predicted taken but later resolves as not taken if that branch is still unresolved while fetch continues down the predicted path. In the reported failing case, a preceding load delays resolution of the first branch, a later branch or jump on the speculative path is also predicted, and the recovery state for the earlier branch is replaced by the later prediction. Instructions from the wrong path can also remain buffered in the instruction fetch pipeline. When the earlier branch is finally resolved as not taken, the core can resume from the wrong PC and continue with wrong-path instructions, which can send execution into an unintended instruction stream and make the core appear to lock up. The expected behavior is that a predicted-taken branch that resolves as not taken must restart execution from the instruction immediately following that branch, independent of any later predictions, and any buffered instructions from the wrong predicted path must be discarded. This affects the instruction-fetch branch prediction and not-taken mispredict recovery logic.

problem_statement: An instruction bus error in the Ibex instruction-fetch path can be misclassified when it occurs on a 32-bit instruction that starts at a half-word-aligned address, so the instruction spans two 16-bit halves across fetch words. In that case, the fetch logic may treat the faulting instruction as if the first half were a completed 16-bit RISC-V compressed instruction, advance the instruction stream by 2 bytes, and, when SecureIbex's sequential program-counter check is enabled, raise a spurious PC mismatch alarm. The correct behavior is that a fetch error must not cause that unaligned 32-bit instruction to be treated as compressed: the instruction must remain incomplete until both halves are available, and the next sequential PC tracked by the fetch path must advance by 4 bytes rather than 2. This affects the instruction fetch FIFO/front-end and is triggered by a sequential instruction bus error during an unaligned 32-bit instruction fetch.

title: Fix behavior of exceptions in debug mode, document debug CSRs
body:
This PR consists of three small commits which implement the following changes:
- Exceptions in debug mode shall not modify any CSRs. This resolves #168 and is related to #365.
- Document debug CSRs. This resolves #307.

Currently, exceptions and special instructions are handled independent of whether the core is in debug mode or not. This is not correct for a couple of cases. For example, the Debug Spec v0.13.2 states on p.39 that while in debug mode:

As a result, `mepc`, `mcause`, `mtval`, and `mstatus` can be modified even though the core is already in Debug Mode. The affected functionality is the Debug Mode exception/CSR handling logic. I'm executing some tests after booting Ibex into User-Mode, and asserting debug stimulus, and I see the following:
![Screenshot from 2019-11-12 17-28-49](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/16736281/68725023-01090380-0572-11ea-86a8-d11f863ff425.png)

Best,
Udi

resolved_issues.title: DMEM fault during misaligned memory access
resolved_issues.body:
Hi all,
When running this set of instructions:
![Screenshot from 2019-10-04 16-43-38](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/16736281/66245995-26c70100-e6c6-11e9-8347-b284c658e62c.png)
The following waves were generated:
![Screenshot from 2019-10-04 16-47-11](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/16736281/66246078-a1901c00-e6c6-11e9-839a-a188fce292f5.png)
The `sw` instructions at `PC=0x800058d0` has a misaligned memory address, and is thus split into two internal memory transactions. In the waves, around 395,800,000ps corresponds to the memory response to the first of these two transactions, which is when the testbench randomly asserts a memory fault here. According to Ibex documentation for this situation, the second memory transaction should continue as normal, ignoring the response data, and then the core needs to also jump to the corresponding fault handler (located at `PC=0x80014000` in our case). The LSU's FSM transitions to it's error handling states from the misaligned transaction states, and the core jumps to `0x80014000` (which encodes the instruction `j 80014080`) directly after `0x800058d0`, but while executing this jump instruction, the core jumps to `0x8001e112` instead, throwing an illegal instruction exception, and then proceeds to wait for the `rvalid` corresponding to the second part of the original misaligned transaction. This occurs around 395,835,000ps, and after this, the core jumps back to the fault handler, and fully executes it. This intermediate PC of `0x8001e112` is calculated as the incorrect jump address from load address data that's already in the execution pipeline, and is muxed through due to `lsu_addr_incr_req_i` going high while waiting for the second half of the misaligned memory transaction to complete. Maybe a potential solution for this would be to only jump to the fault handler after the second part of the misaligned transactions has completed?
Best,
Udi

problem_statement: Recent instruction-side logic and prefetch-buffer changes broke the instruction fetch handshake in Ibex. The instruction-side prefetch buffer issues fetches through a request/grant/response interface: `instr_req_o` requests an instruction fetch, `instr_gnt_i` accepts that request, and the returned instruction data arrives later. In the failing behavior, if a fetch request is made and the grant does not arrive immediately, the prefetch buffer can stop treating that fetch as pending and can advance to a different address before the original request has been accepted. This can desynchronize instruction fetches and cause execution to stop early in the tracing example. The affected logic is the instruction-side prefetch buffer and its request/address tracking. When a fetch is pending but has not yet been granted, including the sequential fetch immediately after a granted branch fetch, `instr_req_o` must remain asserted and `instr_addr_o` must remain at the same word-aligned address until `instr_gnt_i` acknowledges that request.

problem_statement: Ibex mishandles misaligned 32-bit stores in the load-store unit. When a store address is not 32-bit aligned and the access must be split across two adjacent 32-bit words, the address and byte-enable calculation for the second memory transaction is incorrect, so the split store does not preserve the original byte lanes. In the failing boundary case, a 32-bit store to an address whose two least significant bits are `01` is not performed as the required pair of aligned writes. The correct behavior is to issue two aligned store transactions that together write the same four bytes as the original store: the first transaction writes byte lanes 1-3 of the lower word, and the second transaction writes byte lane 0 of the next word. This affects the load-store unit and the address generation used for the second part of a misaligned store, and it is triggered by a misaligned 32-bit store that crosses a 32-bit word boundary.
